title: Pediatric Diabetic Ketoacidosis: ISPAD 2022 Protocol, Fluid Resuscitation and Cerebral Edema

steps.title: ISPAD Biochemical Diagnostic Triad for DKA
steps.tx: DKA is defined by hyperglycemia (blood glucose > 200 mg/dL / 11 mmol/L), venous pH < 7.30 or serum bicarbonate < 18 mEq/L, and ketonemia (blood beta-hydroxybutyrate >= 3.0 mmol/L) or moderate/large ketonuria. The **ISPAD biochemical diagnostic triad for DKA** establishes that absolute insulin deficiency triggers uninhibited lipolysis and hepatic oxidation of free fatty acids into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate. Point-of-care capillary beta-hydroxybutyrate provides immediate confirmation.
steps.say: Diabetic ketoacidosis requires blood glucose over two hundred, venous pH under seven point three or bicarbonate under eighteen, and elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate.

steps.title: Severity Stratification by Venous Blood Gas

left.title: Mild to Moderate DKA
points: Mild: venous pH 7.20-7.29, bicarbonate 10-17 mEq/L
Moderate: venous pH 7.10-7.19, bicarbonate 5-9 mEq/L
Managed in high-dependency step-down unit

right.title: Severe DKA Risk Profile
points: Venous pH < 7.10 or serum bicarbonate < 5 mEq/L
Mandates pediatric intensive care admission
High risk for hypoperfusion and cerebral edema

steps.tx: Severity is classified by acidosis: Mild (venous pH 7.20-7.29 or bicarbonate 10-17 mEq/L), Moderate (pH 7.10-7.19 or bicarbonate 5-9 mEq/L), and Severe (venous pH < 7.10 or bicarbonate < 5 mEq/L). Clinical **DKA severity stratification by venous pH** dictates the level of nursing surveillance, frequency of neurologic observations, and intensive care bed placement. Severe cases experience profound intravascular volume depletion requiring cautious staged resuscitation.
steps.say: Diabetic ketoacidosis is stratified by acidosis severity, where a venous pH below seven point one defines severe disease requiring intensive care.

steps.title: Initial Crystalloid Fluid Resuscitation Guidelines

nodes.label:
Assessment of Dehydration
Typically 5-10% volume deficit

Initial Isotonic Crystalloid
10-20 mL/kg over 1-2 hours

Avoid Rapid Overhydration
No boluses > 20 mL/kg

Maintenance + Deficit
Even replacement over 48 hours

steps.tx: Initial fluid resuscitation is 10-20 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid (0.9% normal saline or Plasmalyte) infused over 1-2 hours; rapid large boluses (> 20 mL/kg) are strictly avoided to minimize cerebral edema risk. Calibrating the **Initial fluid bolus volume and timing** restores effective circulating volume, enhances renal perfusion, and lowers plasma osmolality gradually. Total remaining deficit and maintenance are distributed evenly across 48 hours.
steps.say: Resuscitation starts with ten to twenty milliliters per kilogram of isotonic crystalloid over one to two hours, avoiding aggressive rapid boluses.

steps.title: Insulin Infusion Timing and Protocol Strictures

left.title: Bolus Insulin Contraindicated
points: Never administer an IV insulin bolus
Rapid osmolar drop triggers cerebral swelling
Causes abrupt hypokalemia and vascular collapse

right.title: Continuous Regular Infusion
points: Start 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr regular insulin
Delay start until 1 hour of fluid resuscitation
Restores volume before accelerating glucose uptake

steps.tx: Insulin is NEVER administered as an intravenous bolus; continuous regular insulin infusion is started at 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr only after 1 hour of fluid therapy has restored intravascular volume. Emphasizing **No insulin bolus and delayed infusion start** prevents sudden osmotic collapse and cardiovascular compromise while drastically reducing cerebral edema risk. Initiating insulin after fluid expansion allows hemodynamic stabilization before cellular glucose uptake accelerates.
steps.say: Insulin is never given as an intravenous bolus, but infused at zero point zero five to zero point one units per kilo per hour after an hour of fluids.

steps.title: Two-Bag System and Dextrose Thresholds

nodes.label:
Two-Bag System
Bag 1: 0% Dextrose, Bag 2: 10% Dextrose

Sustained Insulin Rate
Continue insulin until ketoacidosis clears

steps.tx: When blood glucose drops below 250-300 mg/dL (14-17 mmol/L), 5-10% dextrose must be added to IV fluids (using the two-bag system) to maintain blood glucose between 150-200 mg/dL while continuing insulin to clear ketoacidosis. Employing the **Two-bag system and dextrose addition threshold** avoids halting or decreasing insulin prematurely, which would perpetuate lipolysis and prolong acidosis. Titrating rates between bag 1 and bag 2 prevents hypoglycemia while clearing ketones.
steps.say: When glucose drops below three hundred, dextrose is added to intravenous fluids using a two-bag system to allow continued insulin infusion.

steps.title: Potassium Repletion Protocol and Electrolyte Timing

left.title: Total Body Depletion
points: Osmotic diuresis wastes potassium in urine
Serum K may appear deceptively normal or high
Acidosis shifts potassium out of cells

right.title: Infusion Additives
points: Add 40 mEq/L potassium upon verified urine output
50% potassium chloride and 50% potassium phosphate
Withhold if serum potassium >= 5.5 mEq/L

steps.tx: Potassium (40 mEq/L as 50% potassium chloride and 50% potassium phosphate) must be added to IV fluids immediately upon establishing urine output and verifying K < 5.5 mEq/L; insulin shifts potassium intracellularly. Observing strict **Potassium repletion timing and composition** is vital because as insulin drives potassium into hepatocytes and myocytes and rehydration dilutes plasma, rapid life-threatening hypokalemia and fatal cardiac dysrhythmias develop if replacement is neglected.
steps.say: Potassium must be added to maintenance fluids once urine output is established, providing forty milliequivalents per liter to avert dangerous hypokalemia.

steps.title: Contraindication of Sodium Bicarbonate Therapy

left.title: Bicarbonate Fallacies
points: Appears to rapidly correct arterial pH
Historically used for profound acidemia
Fails to improve clinical recovery time

right.title: Proven Severe Hazards
points: Paradoxical CSF and central cerebral acidosis
Aggravates acute intracellular hypokalemia
Significantly increases risk of fatal cerebral edema

steps.tx: Bicarbonate therapy is contraindicated in pediatric DKA because it worsens cerebral intracellular acidosis, causes paradoxical CSF acidosis, hypokalemia, and increases cerebral edema risk. Enforcing the **Sodium bicarbonate contraindication** reflects that exogenous bicarbonate generates lipid-soluble carbon dioxide that diffuses readily across the blood-brain barrier while charged bicarbonate remains excluded. Furthermore, bicarbonate shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve leftward, impairing tissue oxygen release.
steps.say: Sodium bicarbonate is contraindicated in pediatric ketoacidosis because it induces paradoxical central nervous system acidosis and worsens cerebral edema risk.

steps.title: Cerebral Edema Recognition and Hyperosmolar Rescue

nodes.label:
Warning Signs
Headache, bradycardia, lethargy, incontinence

Immediate Bedside Intervention
Elevate head of bed to 30 degrees

Hyperosmolar Therapy
3% saline 3-5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg

Defer Imaging
Never delay hyperosmolar rescue for CT

steps.tx: Cerebral edema occurs in 0.5-1% of pediatric DKA, signaled by headache, bradycardia, lethargy, or incontinence; immediately treat with 3% hypertonic saline (3-5 mL/kg over 15 min) or mannitol (0.5-1.0 g/kg) prior to neuroimaging. Rapid response to **Cerebral edema signs and hyperosmolar therapy** recognizes deterioration typically occurring 4-12 hours after starting treatment. Emergency hyperosmolar agents must be drawn and infused immediately at the bedside, without delaying for diagnostic neuroimaging.
steps.say: Suspected cerebral edema demands urgent administration of three percent hypertonic saline or mannitol before sending the child for brain imaging.
